Read this first — your slide file is incomplete

The Chapter 4 PDF (both your copy and the one in the course folder) contains only 11 slides: the motivation part and then "Thank you". The Dix and Shneiderman content that the exam actually tests is not inside that PDF. It lives in Discussion Session 2, slides 27–35. Everything that is missing has been reconstructed here from Discussion Session 2, the StudOn self-test bank, and the graded exams 2020–2024. You do not need to open the slides.

How the exam is scored — this changes how you study

The exam is on StudOn, in a room, 90 minutes, about 33 questions, about 100 points, no calculator. Most questions are lists of sentences with a checkbox in front of each one. You tick the sentences you think are correct.

The scoring rule that matters

You earn points for each checkbox you get right — both for correctly ticking a true sentence and for correctly leaving a false sentence unticked. A wrong tick removes points inside that question, but a question can never go below 0.

What this means for you: knowing which sentences are false is worth exactly as many points as knowing which are true. That is why this file has a Trap Bank. And when you truly do not know: leave it unticked. An unticked false statement is free points; a wrong tick costs you.

Two more facts, both verified across the 2020–2024 papers:

  • The exam repeats itself. Roughly 70–80 % of every paper is the same questions as previous years, often word for word. This chapter's questions have appeared every single year.
  • The answer options are shuffled. Never memorise "the third option". Memorise which description belongs to which name.

The map of this chapter

Each branch below is a real exam question. Gold = it comes back every year, learn the exact wording. Blue = likely, learn the idea. Red = never tested, do not spend time.

The one idea behind the whole chapter

Start here, because everything else follows from it.

A computer system has two sides. The developer knows how it is built inside: the architecture, the states it can be in, what depends on what, what the system cannot do. The user knows none of that. The user only sees the surface — the screen, the buttons, the sounds.

So the user has to guess what is going on inside, using only what is visible. If the surface is designed badly, the guess is wrong, and the user makes errors, gets frustrated, or gives up.

The chapter in one sentence

Because users can only see the surface, we need rules for designing that surface. Chapter 4 gives you two famous sets of rules: Dix's three principles (a way to judge a system) and Shneiderman's three principles including the eight golden rules (a way to build a system).

Some vocabulary you will meet everywhere, defined simply:

WordPlain meaning
UsabilityHow easy and pleasant a system is to use.
PrincipleAn abstract rule. Very general, tells you what to aim for, not how.
Heuristic / golden ruleA more concrete rule of thumb. Closer to "do this".
UI (user interface)Everything the user can touch, see or hear: screen, buttons, sounds.
DialogueThe back-and-forth between user and system, like a conversation.
InteractionOne round of that conversation: user does something, system answers.

1Dix — the three principles3 pts · every year

Format: matching. You get definitions and lists of sub-components, and you assign each one to Learnability, Flexibility or Robustness.

Alan Dix says: if you want to know whether a system supports usability, ask three questions.

Learnability — "can a beginner get started?"

The exam definition, word for word: "The ease with which new users can begin effective interaction and achieve maximal performance."

The give-away words are new users. Only this definition contains them.

Its five sub-components, in plain English:

  • Predictability — looking at the screen now, can I tell what will happen if I click this? (about the future action)
  • Synthesizability — after I did something, can I see what changed? (about the past action). Example: you drag a file into a folder and the file visibly appears there.
  • Familiarity — does my knowledge from the real world help me here? Example: the rubbish-bin icon for deleting, because I know real bins.
  • Generalizability — does what I learned in one place work in another place? Example: Ctrl+C copies in every program.
  • Consistency — similar things look and behave similarly. (This is also its own big exam topic — see section 3.)

Flexibility — "in how many ways can we talk to each other?"

Exam definition: "The multiplicity of ways the user and system exchange information." "Multiplicity" just means "a large number of different ways".

  • Dialogue initiative — who leads the conversation? If the user is free to do what they want, that is user-preemptive (good). If the system blocks you and demands an answer first, that is system-preemptive (a pop-up you must close).
  • Multithreading — can the user do more than one task at a time? (Really at the same time, or by switching back and forth.)
  • Task migratability — can a task be moved between user and system? Example: spell checking. You can do it yourself, or hand it to the computer.
  • Substitutivity — can equivalent things be swapped? Example: typing 5cm or 50mm; seeing your data as a number or as a chart.

Small conflict — and how to handle it

This year's Discussion Session 2 slide also lists Customizability under Flexibility (5 items). The graded exam answer key lists only 4: Dialogue initiative, Multithreading, Task migratability, Substitutivity. The graded exam wins — but if you see "Customizability" as an option in a Flexibility question, it is safe to treat it as belonging to Flexibility too. It never belongs to Learnability or Robustness.

Robustness — "does the system help me succeed and recover?"

Exam definition: "The level of support provided to the user in determining successful achievement and assessment of goal-directed behavior." Translated: does the system help me see whether I reached my goal, and fix things when I did not?

  • Observability — can I see the internal state of the system from what is on the screen? Example: a progress bar tells me the system is working.
  • Recoverability — after an error, can I get back to a good state? Undo, or a "restore" function.
  • Responsiveness — how quickly does the system react, and does it tell me how long it will take?
  • Task conformance — does the system actually support all the tasks I want to do, in the way I want to do them?

The three-second decision rule for the exam

Scan the sentence for one of three words:
  "new users" → Learnability  ·  "multiplicity" / "many ways" → Flexibility  ·  "support" / "assessment" → Robustness

And for the sub-component lists: the list with 5 items is Learnability. The list starting with "Dialogue…" is Flexibility. The list starting with "Observability…" is Robustness.

The trap in this question

In 2021 the options included Likeability. Likeability is not a Dix principle — it comes from Chapter 1 (Utility / Usability / Likeability). Never assign a Dix definition to it.

Real exam question · SS2021 Q4 + StudOn self-test · ≈3 points
Assign the correct description to each principle to support usability by Alan Dix. Available terms: Learnability · Flexibility · Robustness · Likeability
1. "The level of support provided to the user in determining successful achievement and assessment of goal-directed behavior" 2. "Dialogue initiative, Multithreading, Task migratability, Substitutivity" 3. "The ease with which new users can begin effective interaction and achieve maximal performance" 4. "Observability, Recoverability, Task conformance, Responsiveness" 5. "The multiplicity of ways the user and system exchange information" 6. "Predictability, Synthesizability, Familiarity, Generalizability, Consistency"
Show the graded answer
1 → Robustness — the words "support" and "assessment".
2 → Flexibility — the list beginning with "Dialogue…".
3 → Learnability — the words "new users".
4 → Robustness — the list beginning with "Observability…".
5 → Flexibility — the word "multiplicity".
6 → Learnability — the list of five, ending with Consistency.
Likeability is used for nothing. It is a distractor.

2Shneiderman — the eight golden rules2 – 10 pts

Format: multiple choice about the rules, and — the big one — a scenario where features of an app are described and you must say which golden rule each feature follows. In SS2023 this single question was worth 10 points.

Ben Shneiderman gives three principles for designing user interfaces:

  1. Recognize user diversity — your users are not all the same (see section 6).
  2. Follow the eight golden rules — this section.
  3. Prevent errors — understand the errors people make (see section 4).

What each rule means, in plain English

RuleWhat it asks you to doReal example
1. Strive for consistencyThe same things should look and be named the same everywhere. Different words should not mean the same thing.All icons follow one colour scheme.
2. Enable frequent users to use shortcutsExperts should be able to skip the long way.A swipe gesture jumps straight to the detail view.
3. Offer informative feedbackAlways tell the user what the system is doing and what happened.A message shows the result of the last action; the navigation bar shows which view is open.
4. Design dialogues to yield closureEvery task should have a clear beginning, middle and end. The end must be announced."Test successful" appears when the measurement is finished.
5. Error prevention / handlingStop errors before they happen; if they happen, explain them and how to fix them.The app checks whether a typed value is plausible before accepting it.
6. Permit easy reversal of actionsThe user must be able to undo.A button deletes the last measurement.
7. Support internal locus of controlThe user must feel they are in charge. The system should not surprise them or act on its own.The user starts the data transfer themselves; the app asks "save this configuration?".
8. Reduce short-term memory loadDo not force the user to remember things between steps. Show it on screen.The start screen shows all relevant values; instructions stay visible.

"Locus of control" — the phrase that confuses everyone

Locus means "place". Internal locus of control = the user feels the control sits inside them: "I made this happen." The rule says: design so the user initiates the actions and is never surprised. Exam trap: "the system should initiate the actions" is FALSE — the user should.

"Closure" — the other confusing word

Closure = finishing. A dialogue "yields closure" when the user gets a clear signal that the task is complete. The 2021 exam asked about the golden rules "including background knowledge of Closure". Do not confuse this with the Gestalt law of closure from the Humans chapter, which is about seeing incomplete shapes as whole — same word, different topic.

The graded pairings from the SS2023 exam (10 points)

These are the actual feature descriptions and the rule each one was graded as. This is the highest-value table in the whole chapter.

Feature described in the examGraded golden rule
All icons use a predefined colour schemeStrive for consistency
"Different words or actions should not mean the same thing"Strive for consistency
Familiar users reach a detailed view by a gesture / shortcutEnable frequent users to use shortcuts
The user learns the current system status / the outcome of previous interactionsOffer informative feedback
The navigation bar shows which view is currently openOffer informative feedback (not memory load!)
A "test successful" message at the end; actions have beginning, middle and endDesign dialogues to yield closure
A plausibility check on manual inputs; clear error messages with hintsError prevention / handling
A button that deletes the last measurementPermit easy reversal of actions
Users start the data transfer themselves; "users don't want surprises"Support internal locus of control
Asking "save this configuration?" / "confirm password change?"Support internal locus of control (not reversal, not shortcuts!)
The start screen reminds the user of all relevant parameters; instructions stay visibleReduce short-term memory load

The two pairings that cost students points in 2023

  • "The navigation bar shows which view is open" feels like memory load, but it was graded as informative feedback — the system is telling you the current state.
  • "Do you want to save this configuration?" feels like reversal or a shortcut, but it was graded as locus of control — the system asks permission instead of acting alone.
Real exam question · SS2023 style · scenario matching · up to 10 points
A health app (ProHerz) is described. Assign the correct golden rule to each feature.
a) The app shows the message "Test successful" once the measurement is complete. b) A plausibility check warns the user when a typed blood-pressure value is impossible. c) The user must press "send" themselves before any data leaves the phone. d) The home screen displays all values the user needs for the next step. e) Experienced users open the detail view with a swipe instead of three taps.
Show the graded answer
a → Design dialogues to yield closure (the task is announced as finished)
b → Error prevention / handling
c → Support internal locus of control (the user initiates, no surprises)
d → Reduce short-term memory load (nothing to remember)
e → Enable frequent users to use shortcuts

3Consistency — three levels3 – 6 pts · every year

Format: multiple choice or matching, usually built around Apple's user interface (the 1980s Macintosh compared with a modern Mac).

Consistency means: the same thing always behaves and looks the same. But there are three different levels of "same", and the exam tests exactly this distinction.

  • Lexical consistency — always the same word, colour or shape for the same object. ("Lexical" comes from lexicon = dictionary, so it is about the vocabulary.) Example: red always means "no/stop", green always means "yes/go"; the menu is always called "File", never sometimes "Document".
  • Syntactic consistency — always the same order and structure. ("Syntax" = the order of words in a sentence.) Example: the menu bar is always File → Edit → View → … → Help, in that order, in every program.
  • Semantic consistency — always the same meaning. ("Semantics" = meaning.) Example: "Help" always opens help, everywhere; "File" always gives you options about the file you are working on right now.

Memory hook

Lexical = the word. Syntactic = the order. Semantic = the meaning.
Ask yourself: is the sentence talking about what it is called / what colour it is (lexical), where it sits in the sequence (syntactic), or what it does (semantic)?

The three Apple sentences that were graded FALSE in 2021 and 2022

These come back. Learn them as false:

  • FALSE "The Apple logo is always in the top-left corner — this is lexical consistency." → Position in a sequence is not vocabulary.
  • FALSE "The Help option is always present — this is syntactic consistency." → That "Help" always means help is about meaning.
  • FALSE "The close button is always red — this is semantic consistency." → Always the same colour for the same object is lexical.

What is graded true: "the same words are used, like File, Edit, View" = lexical.

Real exam question · appears every year · ≈3 points
Looking at the Apple user interface from 1980 and from 2010, choose the correct statements.
a) The menu bar always shows the same words (File, Edit, View) — this is lexical consistency. b) The Apple logo is always in the top-left corner — this is lexical consistency. c) The order of the menu entries has not changed — this is syntactic consistency. d) The close button is always red — this is semantic consistency. e) "Help" always opens the help function — this is semantic consistency.
Show the graded answer
a → TICK — same words = lexical.
b → DO NOT TICK — graded false. Position is not lexical.
c → TICK — same order = syntactic.
d → DO NOT TICK — graded false. Same colour for the same object = lexical.
e → TICK — same meaning = semantic.
Remember: the two you correctly leave unticked earn points too.

4Slips and mistakes1 – 3 pts

Format: matching. Six descriptions, six type names. This is Shneiderman's third principle, "Prevent errors": to prevent errors you must first know which errors humans make.

The top-level split (this alone has been a 1-point question)

  • Slip = right goal, wrong action. You knew what you wanted; your body or habit did something else. It is the result of automatic behaviour.
  • Mistake = wrong goal. You planned the wrong thing in the first place — overgeneralization, wrong conclusions.

The six types of slips

Learn them by their little story — the exam reuses the same stories every year.

TypeExam description (learn this wording)Story to remember it
Capture errorTwo actions with a common start point; the more familiar one captures the unusual one.Driving to work on Saturday instead of to the supermarket.
Description errorPerforming an action that is close to the action one wanted to perform.Putting the cutlery in the bin instead of the sink.
Data-driven errorUsing data that is visible in a particular moment instead of the data that is well known.Calling the room number you can see instead of the phone number you know by heart.
Associate action errorYou think of something and that thought influences your action.Saying "come in!" after picking up the phone.
Loss-of-activation error (= forgetting)You decided to do something, but when you leave you forget what it was. Going back to the start place, you remember.Walking into the kitchen and forgetting why.
Mode errorYou forget that you are in a mode that does not allow a certain action, or where an action has a different effect.Typing your password with CAPS LOCK on.

Important — an error on this year's slide

Discussion Session 2, slide 32, describes data-driven errors as "When users return to the design after a period of not using it, how easily can they reestablish proficiency?" That is not a slip at all — it is the definition of memorability (Nielsen). It is a copy-paste error on the slide. Use the exam wording instead: data-driven error = using data visible right now instead of the data you know.

Mnemonic for the order

C – D – D – A – L – M : Capture, Description, Data-driven, Associate, Loss-of-activation, Mode. A sentence to hold it: "Cars Drive Down A Long Motorway."

Real exam question · SS2020, SS2021 Q14, SS2022, SS2024 · ≈3 points
Assign the correct description to each type of slip.
a) "You forget that you are in a mode that does not allow a certain action." b) "Two actions with a common start point, the more familiar one captures the unusual." c) "You think of something and that influences your action." d) "Performing an action that is close to the action that one wanted to perform." e) "Using data that is visible in a particular moment instead of the data that is well-known." f) "In a given environment you decided to do something, but when leaving you forgot what you wanted to do."
Show the graded answer
a → Mode error
b → Capture error
c → Associate action error
d → Description error
e → Data-driven error
f → Loss-of-activation error (forgetting)

5Types of design rules1 – 2 pts

Format: label the diagram (SS2021 Q11: "Name types of design in diagram").

Design rules come in different strengths. Two things change as you move along the scale:

  • Generality — how widely the rule applies. High generality = it applies to almost any system, but it does not tell you exactly what to do.
  • Authority — how strongly you must obey it. High authority = you must follow it exactly.

These two always move in opposite directions: the more general a rule, the less it can command you; the more precise a rule, the narrower its scope.

NameDefinition (exam wording)
PrinciplesAbstract design rules.
Golden rules and heuristicsMore concrete than principles.
Standards(Very) detailed design rules.
Design patternsGeneric solution for a specific problem.
Style guidesProvided for devices, operating systems, widget libraries.

Mnemonic

P – G – S – D – S: "Principles Give Standards, Designers Style." And remember which end is which: Principles sit top-left (most general, least authority), style guides sit bottom-right (least general, most authority).

Real exam question · SS2021 Q11 · ≈2 points
The diagram shows generality on the vertical axis and authority on the horizontal axis, with five points along a diagonal from top-left to bottom-right. Name them in order.
Show the graded answer
1. Principles
2. Golden rules (and heuristics)
3. Standards
4. Design patterns
5. Style guides

6User diversity and personas2 – 3 pts

Format: multiple choice, "choose the right statements". This is Shneiderman's Principle 1.

Recognize user diversity means: the people who will use your system are not all the same. They differ in age, experience, culture, language, physical ability, and in what they want to achieve. A design that only fits one type of person fails for the others.

The tool used to handle this is the persona.

What a persona is

A persona is an invented person who stands for one important group of real users. It has a name, an age, a job, goals and frustrations — but it is not a real individual, and it is not the average user. Designers use it to role-play: "would Anna understand this screen?"

The course says it directly: there is no "average" user. The goal of personas is to characterize the important end-user groups, and to answer the question "Who are we designing for?"

Real exam question · SS2022, SS2023 · also Discussion Session 5 slide 28 · ≈3 points
Personas are created for this system. Choose the right statements in the context of interaction design.
a) A persona is used to role-play through an interface design. b) A persona is a real person. c) A persona represents a particular type of user. d) A persona represents the average German person.
Show the graded answer
a → TICK
b → DO NOT TICK — a persona is fictional.
c → TICK — a particular type, i.e. a user group.
d → DO NOT TICK — "there is no average user" is the course's own sentence.

7UI versus UX2 pts

Format: multiple choice statements. Appeared three times in the SS2023 paper family.

  • UI (User Interface design) — "this is how it looks like". Anything a user may interact with to use a digital product or service: screens, touchscreens, keyboards, sounds, lights. UI enhances the look and function of a product, focusing on tangible elements (things you can point at).
  • UX (User Experience design) — "this is how it feels like". Don Norman and Jakob Nielsen's definition: "all aspects of the end-user's interaction with the company, its services, and its products." UX is about the user's whole problem-solving journey: their needs and the challenges they face.

The recurring trap

FALSE: "You cannot create a UX." The graded logic is the opposite — you cannot NOT create a user experience. Every product produces some experience, good or bad. Your only choice is whether you design it on purpose.

Also note: UX is wider than UI. UI is one part of UX, not the same thing, and not the other way round.

8The motivation slides0 pts — never tested

Slides 3–10 of the chapter (the Big Ben clock, "users only see what is visible", and the three different answers to "what do you see on this desktop?") have never appeared in any exam from 2020 to 2024. Read this box once and move on — that is all the time they deserve.

In 30 seconds: A clock face shows you the time, but hides the machinery behind it. Software is the same. Users only see what is visible; they have little idea about the architecture, state transitions, dependencies, application context and system restrictions — and usually they do not even know that these things exist.

Asked "what do you see on a computer desktop?", three kinds of people answer differently:

  • Skilled computer user: icons, toolbars, overlapping windows, scroll bars, menus, a pointer.
  • Naive technical answer: a 2-D surface of controllable pixels, e.g. 1400×1050, each pixel's colour can be set and changed rapidly.
  • The "perfect" user: my work environment — meeting notes, next year's budget, a request to write an article.

The point: the last answer is the one that matters, because people think in tasks, not in pixels or windows.

Money Sheet — everything you must be able to write from a blank page

A · Dix

PrincipleDefinition (exact)Sub-componentsMnemonic
LearnabilityThe ease with which new users can begin effective interaction and achieve maximal performancePredictability, Synthesizability, Familiarity, Generalizability, ConsistencyP S F G C — "Please Study For Good Consistency"
FlexibilityThe multiplicity of ways the user and system exchange informationDialogue initiative, Multithreading, Task migratability, SubstitutivityD M T S — "Dialogues Migrate To Substitutes"
RobustnessThe level of support provided to the user in determining successful achievement and assessment of goal-directed behaviorObservability, Recoverability, Task conformance, ResponsivenessO R T R — "Observe, Recover, Task, Respond"

B · The eight golden rules, in order

1 Strive for consistency · 2 Enable frequent users to use shortcuts · 3 Offer informative feedback · 4 Design dialogues to yield closure · 5 Error prevention / handling · 6 Permit easy reversal of actions · 7 Support internal locus of control · 8 Reduce short-term memory load.

Story mnemonic: A shop that is always the same (1) has a fast lane for regulars (2), a cashier who tells you what is happening (3) and says "done!" at the end (4). It stops you buying the wrong thing (5), takes returns (6), never decides for you (7), and puts a note in your bag so you don't have to remember (8).

C · Consistency

Lexical = same word / colour / shape. Syntactic = same order. Semantic = same meaning.

D · Slips

Slip = right goal, wrong action (automatic behaviour). Mistake = wrong goal, overgeneralization, wrong conclusions.
Six types: Capture · Description · Data-driven · Associate action · Loss-of-activation · Mode.

E · Design rules, in order along the diagonal

Principles → Golden rules & heuristics → Standards → Design patterns → Style guides.
Vertical axis = increasing generality, horizontal axis = increasing authority.

F · Shneiderman's three principles

1 Recognize user diversity · 2 Follow the eight golden rules · 3 Prevent errors.

G · Personas

Fictional · represents a user type/group · used to role-play a design · not a real person · not the average user · "there is no average user".

H · UI vs UX

UI = how it looks, tangible elements. UX = how it feels, all aspects of the end-user's interaction with the company, its services and its products (Norman & Nielsen).

Trap Bank — the recurring FALSE statements

Every sentence below has been graded false. Leaving them unticked earns you points. Read this list out loud twice a week — it is also your English practice, because the exam reuses these exact sentences.

The false statementWhy it is false
"Likeability is one of Dix's principles."Dix has three: Learnability, Flexibility, Robustness. Likeability belongs to Chapter 1.
"Consistency is a sub-component of Robustness."It is a sub-component of Learnability.
"Observability belongs to Flexibility."Observability belongs to Robustness.
"Locus of control means the system should initiate the actions."The opposite — the user must feel in control and initiate.
"Error handling means basically all actions should be reversible (UNDO)."That describes permit easy reversal of actions (rule 6), not error handling (rule 5).
"The navigation bar showing the current view reduces short-term memory load."Graded as informative feedback.
"Asking 'save this configuration?' is an example of easy reversal / of a shortcut."Graded as internal locus of control.
"The Apple logo always top-left is lexical consistency."Graded false. Lexical is about words, colours and shapes of the object itself.
"The always-present Help option is syntactic consistency."Graded false — that Help always means help is semantic.
"The red close button is semantic consistency."Graded false — same colour for the same object is lexical.
"A persona is a real person." / "A persona represents the average person."A persona is fictional and represents a type. There is no average user.
"You cannot create a UX."You cannot not create one — every product creates an experience.
"Data-driven error = how easily users regain proficiency after not using the design."That is memorability. Data-driven = using data visible now instead of data you know. (Slide 32 has this wrong.)
"A slip means the user chose the wrong goal."Slip = right goal, wrong action. Wrong goal = mistake.
"Standards are more general than principles."Reverse. Principles are the most general and the least binding.

New-question radar — where a NEW question would come from

Why this section exists: in 2024 the exam added a brand-new question about the Chinese Room argument — exactly in the year AI content was added to the slides. New questions follow new or untested slides. These are the untested corners of Chapter 4. Understand them; do not memorise tick patterns, because a new question is usually a reworded or inverted version.

Radar 1 · "What the developer knows" — the visibility gap

5-minute understanding: the user sees only the surface. Five things stay invisible to them: architecture (how the system is built), state transitions (which state it moves to next), dependencies (what needs what), application context (what situation it is used in), system restrictions (what it cannot do). And users usually do not even know these exist — so they cannot ask about them. This is why we need design rules at all.

A question I would write: "Users have little idea about which aspects of a system? Choose the correct statements." — with architecture, state transitions, dependencies, application context, system restrictions as true and things like "the colour of the buttons" or "the position of the menu" as false (those are visible).

Radar 2 · The three answers to "what do you see?"

5-minute understanding: the same screen produces three descriptions — the skilled user lists interface objects, the naive technical answer lists pixels and resolution, the perfect user lists tasks and documents. The teaching point: good design must serve the third view, because people care about their work, not about windows.

A question I would write: a matching question — assign "2D image with a resolution of 1400×1050", "overlapping windows and scroll bars", "budget for next year and meeting notes" to Basic (naive) technical answer / Skilled computer user answer / Perfect user's answer.

Radar 3 · Customizability (new on this year's Flexibility slide)

5-minute understanding: customizability means the interface can be modified by the user or by the system. If the user changes it, that is adaptability. If the system changes itself automatically, that is adaptivity. It belongs to Flexibility because it is another way of varying how user and system exchange information.

A question I would write: "Which of the following are sub-components of Flexibility?" including Customizability as a true option and Observability / Consistency as false ones.

Radar 4 · Definitions of the design-rule types as a cloze

5-minute understanding: so far this was only ever a "label the diagram" question. The easiest new variant is to give the definition and ask for the name, or the reverse. Be able to go both ways: abstract design rules ↔ principles; more concrete than principles ↔ golden rules and heuristics; (very) detailed design rules ↔ standards; generic solution for a specific problem ↔ design patterns; provided for devices, operating systems, widget libraries ↔ style guides.

A question I would write: "A generic solution for a specific problem is called a ______." (Answer: design pattern.)

Radar 5 · Dialogue initiative: user-preemptive vs system-preemptive

5-minute understanding: in a dialogue somebody must speak first. User-preemptive = the user is free to choose the next action; this is generally preferred. System-preemptive = the system takes the initiative and restricts the user, for example a modal dialog box that must be answered before anything else can happen. Sometimes system-preemptive is right: for dangerous or irreversible actions.

A question I would write: "A pop-up window blocks the interface until the user confirms. Which term describes this dialogue?" (Answer: system-preemptive dialogue initiative.)

Radar 6 · Shneiderman's Principle 1 beyond personas

5-minute understanding: "recognize user diversity" covers more than personas: novice vs knowledgeable intermittent vs expert frequent users; differences in age, culture, language and physical ability. A design usually needs layers: simple defaults for novices plus shortcuts for experts — which is exactly why golden rule 2 exists.

A question I would write: "Which design decisions follow from recognizing user diversity? Choose the correct statements." with "offer both a guided wizard and keyboard shortcuts" true and "design for the average user" false.

Mock exam — 12 questions in the real formats

Answer each one before you open the reveal. Score yourself the way StudOn does: one point fraction per checkbox you get right, including the ones you correctly leave empty.

Q1 · matching · 3 pts
Assign: Learnability / Flexibility / Robustness.
a) Observability, Recoverability, Task conformance, Responsiveness b) The multiplicity of ways the user and system exchange information c) Predictability, Synthesizability, Familiarity, Generalizability, Consistency
Show the graded answer
a → Robustness · b → Flexibility · c → Learnability
Q2 · multiple choice · 2 pts
Which statements about Dix's principles are correct?
a) Consistency is a sub-component of Learnability. b) Likeability is the fourth principle. c) Task migratability means a task can be passed between user and system. d) Recoverability belongs to Flexibility.
Show the graded answer
a TICK · b leave empty (not a Dix principle) · c TICK · d leave empty (it belongs to Robustness)
Q3 · cloze · 1 pt
Complete: "Learnability is the ease with which ______ can begin effective interaction and achieve maximal performance."
Show the graded answer
new users
Q4 · name the list · 4 pts
Name the eight golden rules.
Show the graded answer
1 Strive for consistency · 2 Enable frequent users to use shortcuts · 3 Offer informative feedback · 4 Design dialogues to yield closure · 5 Error prevention / handling · 6 Permit easy reversal of actions · 7 Support internal locus of control · 8 Reduce short-term memory load
Q5 · scenario matching · 5 pts
A smart-home dashboard. Assign the golden rule to each feature.
a) After changing a setting the app shows "Configuration saved". b) All warning icons use the same red across every screen. c) The app never switches the heating on by itself; the user confirms. d) An "undo" arrow restores the previous temperature. e) The current room is always shown in the header, so the user need not remember it.
Show the graded answer
a → Offer informative feedback (or closure, if the sentence says the task is finished — here it reports a result, so feedback)
b → Strive for consistency
c → Support internal locus of control
d → Permit easy reversal of actions
e → Reduce short-term memory load
Q6 · multiple choice · 2 pts
Which statements about the golden rules are correct?
a) Supporting internal locus of control means the system should take the initiative. b) Closure means the user gets a clear signal that a task is complete. c) Error prevention means that all actions should be reversible. d) Shortcuts are meant for frequent users.
Show the graded answer
a leave empty — the user takes the initiative.
b TICK
c leave empty — that is rule 6, not rule 5.
d TICK
Q7 · multiple choice · 3 pts
Apple's user interface, 1980 versus 2010. Which statements are correct?
a) The same menu words (File, Edit, View) are used — lexical consistency. b) The Apple logo is always top-left — lexical consistency. c) The menu order never changed — syntactic consistency. d) The close button is always red — semantic consistency.
Show the graded answer
a TICK · b leave empty · c TICK · d leave empty
Q8 · matching · 2 pts
Assign to Slips or Mistakes.
a) "Right goal but wrong action, result of automatic behaviour" b) "Wrong goal, overgeneralization, wrong conclusions"
Show the graded answer
a → Slips · b → Mistakes
Q9 · matching · 3 pts
Name the slip type.
a) You drive towards your office although today you wanted to go to the supermarket. b) You dial the room number printed on the door instead of the phone number you know. c) Your text appears in capitals because you did not notice CAPS LOCK.
Show the graded answer
a → Capture error · b → Data-driven error · c → Mode error
Q10 · label the diagram · 2 pts
Five types of design rules, from most general to most authoritative.
Show the graded answer
Principles → Golden rules and heuristics → Standards → Design patterns → Style guides
Q11 · multiple choice · 2 pts
Which statements about personas are correct?
a) A persona represents a particular type of user. b) A persona must be based on one real person. c) Personas are used to role-play through an interface design. d) A persona describes the average user.
Show the graded answer
a TICK · b leave empty · c TICK · d leave empty
Q12 · multiple choice · 2 pts
Which statements about UI and UX are correct?
a) UI focuses on tangible elements such as screens, keyboards and sounds. b) UX covers all aspects of the end-user's interaction with the company, its services and its products. c) You cannot create a UX. d) UI and UX are two words for the same thing.
Show the graded answer
a TICK · b TICK · c leave empty — you cannot not create one · d leave empty

Flashcards to make (front = exam wording, back = graded answer)

"The ease with which new users can begin effective interaction and achieve maximal performance"
Learnability
"The multiplicity of ways the user and system exchange information"
Flexibility
"The level of support provided to the user in determining successful achievement and assessment of goal-directed behavior"
Robustness
Sub-components of Learnability
Predictability, Synthesizability, Familiarity, Generalizability, Consistency
Sub-components of Flexibility
Dialogue initiative, Multithreading, Task migratability, Substitutivity
Sub-components of Robustness
Observability, Recoverability, Task conformance, Responsiveness
The eight golden rules, in order
Consistency · Shortcuts · Informative feedback · Closure · Error prevention/handling · Easy reversal · Internal locus of control · Reduce short-term memory load
"The navigation bar shows which view is currently open" → which golden rule?
Offer informative feedback (NOT reduce memory load)
"Do you want to save this configuration?" → which golden rule?
Support internal locus of control (NOT easy reversal)
Lexical / syntactic / semantic consistency
same word, colour, shape / same order / same meaning
Slip vs mistake
Slip = right goal, wrong action (automatic behaviour). Mistake = wrong goal, overgeneralization, wrong conclusions.
The six slip types
Capture, Description, Data-driven, Associate action, Loss-of-activation, Mode
Five types of design rules, general → authoritative
Principles, Golden rules & heuristics, Standards, Design patterns, Style guides
Shneiderman's three principles
Recognize user diversity · Follow the eight golden rules · Prevent errors
Is a persona a real person?
No — fictional, represents a user type/group; there is no average user
UI vs UX in one line each
UI = how it looks (tangible elements). UX = how it feels (all aspects of the end-user's interaction with the company, its services and products)

Final self-check

Tick these on paper. Anything you cannot do goes back into tomorrow's 20 minutes.

  • I can write the three Dix principles with their exact definitions.
  • I can write all thirteen sub-components in the right groups.
  • I can name the eight golden rules in order without looking.
  • Given a described app feature, I can name the golden rule — including the two traps (navigation bar → feedback; "save this?" → locus of control).
  • I can explain lexical, syntactic and semantic consistency with one example each, and I know the three false Apple sentences.
  • I can match all six slip types to their stories, and explain slip vs mistake.
  • I can draw the design-rules diagram with both axis labels and all five names.
  • I can pick the true persona statements and say why "average user" is wrong.
  • I can state UI vs UX and why "you cannot create a UX" is false.
  • I read the whole Trap Bank out loud without hesitating over the English.

How to use this file from now on

Day 1: read it once, top to bottom, without trying to memorise. Day 2: do the Mock Exam with the reveals closed, then re-read only the sections you got wrong. Day 3 onwards: 15 minutes — Money Sheet from a blank page, then the Trap Bank out loud. Repeat twice a week until 11 September. Do not open the slides.
